Numerical Quantum Mechanics

TDSE

The one-dimensional time-dependent Schrodinger equation is given by :

−ℏ22m∂2∂x2ψ(x,t)+V(x,t)ψ(x,t)=iℏ∂∂tψ(x,t)\frac{-\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \psi(x,t) + V(x,t)\psi(x,t) = i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi(x,t) 2m−ℏ2​∂x2∂2​ψ(x,t)+V(x,t)ψ(x,t)=iℏ∂t∂​ψ(x,t)

V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0

In this case, we have :

−ℏ22m∂2∂x2ψ=iℏ∂∂tψ  ⟹  ∂∂tψ=(iℏ2m)∂2∂x2ψ\begin{aligned} \frac{-\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \psi &= i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi \\ \implies \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi= (\frac{i\hbar}{2m})\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}\psi \end{aligned} 2m−ℏ2​∂x2∂2​ψ⟹∂t∂​ψ=(2miℏ​)∂x2∂2​ψ​=iℏ∂t∂​ψ

By separation of variables, i.e. ψ(x,t)=a(x)b(t)\psi(x,t) = a(x)b(t)ψ(x,t)=a(x)b(t), we get :

a(x)b′(t)=(iℏ2m)a′′(x)b(t)a(x)b'(t) = (\frac{i\hbar}{2m}) a''(x)b(t) a(x)b′(t)=(2miℏ​)a′′(x)b(t)

Then, for all (x,t)(x,t)(x,t) where a≠0a\ne 0a=0 and b≠0b \ne 0b=0, we have:

b′(t)b(t)=(iℏ2m)a′′(x)a(x)[=f(x,t)]\frac{b'(t)}{b(t)} = (\frac{i\hbar}{2m}) \frac{a''(x)}{a(x)} \quad [= f (x,t)] b(t)b′(t)​=(2miℏ​)a(x)a′′(x)​[=f(x,t)]

Since LHS is a constant w.r.t xxx and RHS is constant w.r.t ttt, we can say set both equal to some constant −iω-i \omega−iω. So, we get :

b′(t)=−iωb(t)ℏ2ma′′(x)=−ωa(x)b'(t) = -i\omega b(t) \\ \frac{\hbar}{2m} a''(x) = -\omega a(x) b′(t)=−iωb(t)2mℏ​a′′(x)=−ωa(x)

These equations are easy to solve. We get the solution

b(t)=βe−iωta(x)=α1ei2mℏωx+α2e−i2mℏωxb(t) = \beta e^{-i\omega t} \\ a(x) = \alpha_1 e^{i\sqrt{\frac{2m}{\hbar}\omega} x} + \alpha_2 e^{-i\sqrt{\frac{2m}{\hbar} \omega} x} b(t)=βe−iωta(x)=α1​eiℏ2m​ω​x+α2​e−iℏ2m​ω​x

Now, for stability and boundedness of these solutions, it is necessary that ω∈R+\omega\in \mathbb{R}^{+}ω∈R+.

Of-course, this is only a solution, and we can have as many as we want for all the different values of ω\omegaω.

Therefore, we have a basis of solutions, namely:

ψk(x,t)=Akei(kx−ωt)whereω=ℏ2mk2andk∈R\psi_k(x,t) = A_k e^{i(kx -\omega t)} \quad \text{where}\quad \omega=\frac{\hbar}{2m}k^2 \quad \text{and} \quad k\in \mathbb{R} ψk​(x,t)=Ak​ei(kx−ωt)whereω=2mℏ​k2andk∈R

This gives the general solution:

ψ(x,t)=∫−∞∞[12πϕ(k)]ei(kx−ωt)dk\psi(x,t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} [\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \phi(k)] e^{i(kx-\omega t)} dk ψ(x,t)=∫−∞∞​[2π​1​ϕ(k)]ei(kx−ωt)dk

Set t=0t=0t=0 (which can be any point you want really) and this looks like an inverse fourier transform.

From this, it's easy to see that:

ϕ(k)=12π∫−∞∞ψ(x,0)e−ikxdx\phi(k) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \psi(x,0) e^{-ikx}dx ϕ(k)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​ψ(x,0)e−ikxdx

Now, since we did the whole setting t=0t=0t=0 think without realling caring about what point in time we are choosing as t=0t=0t=0, we effectively dissolved the e−iωte^{-i\omega t}e−iωt into ϕ(k)\phi(k)ϕ(k). So, it's better to actually think of it that and not do the t=0t=0t=0 trick. This gives us :

ψ(x,t)=12π∫−∞∞ϕ(k,t)eikxdk=F−1[ϕ]ϕ(k,t)=12π∫−∞∞ψ(x,t)e−ikxdx=F[ψ]\psi(x,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi(k,t) e^{ikx}dk = {\cal F}^{-1}[\phi] \\ \phi(k,t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \psi(x,t) e^{-ikx}dx = {\cal F}[\psi] \\ ψ(x,t)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​ϕ(k,t)eikxdk=F−1[ϕ]ϕ(k,t)=2π​1​∫−∞∞​ψ(x,t)e−ikxdx=F[ψ]

If we use the 2nd equation to define ϕ\phiϕ, then these two equations are mathematically true in general, not just for V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0

The only think special about the V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0 case is that we can write

ϕ(k,t)=ϕ(k,0)e−iℏ2mk2t\phi(k,t) = \phi(k,0)e^{-i \frac{\hbar}{2m}k^2 t} ϕ(k,t)=ϕ(k,0)e−i2mℏ​k2t

That is to say, once the initial conditions are given, we have an analytical solution for the evolution.

Momentum and Position

In quantum mechanics, any observable quantity O(t)O(t)O(t) is represented by an Hermitian operator O^\hat OO^, i.e. one that has the property ⟨O^ψ1∣ψ2⟩=⟨ψ1∣O^ψ2⟩\braket{ \hat O \psi_1 | \psi_2} = \braket{\psi_1 |\hat O \psi_2}⟨O^ψ1​∣ψ2​⟩=⟨ψ1​∣O^ψ2​⟩ where the "bra-ket" notation is defined as :

⟨ψ1∣ψ2⟩=∫−∞∞ψ1∗(x,t)ψ2∗(x,t)dx\braket{\psi_1|\psi_2} = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi_1^*(x,t)\psi_2^*(x,t) dx ⟨ψ1​∣ψ2​⟩=∫−∞∞​ψ1∗​(x,t)ψ2∗​(x,t)dx

In fact, we in particular have the expectation (mean) value:

⟨O⟩(t)=⟨ψ(t)∣O^∣ψ(t)⟩=⟨ψ∣O^ψ⟩\braket{O}(t) = \bra {\psi(t)} \hat O \ket{\psi(t)} = \braket{\psi| \hat O \psi} ⟨O⟩(t)=⟨ψ(t)∣O^∣ψ(t)⟩=⟨ψ∣O^ψ⟩

For position, the operator is x^=x\hat x = xx^=x. Thus,

⟨x⟩(t)=∫−∞∞ψ∗(x,t) x ψ(x,t) dx=∫−∞∞x∣ψ(x,t)∣2dx=E[x](t)\braket{x}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi^*(x,t) \,x\,\psi(x,t) \,dx = \int_{-\infty}^\infty x |\psi(x,t)|^2 dx = E[x](t) ⟨x⟩(t)=∫−∞∞​ψ∗(x,t)xψ(x,t)dx=∫−∞∞​x∣ψ(x,t)∣2dx=E[x](t)

For momentum ppp, we have p^=ℏi∂∂x\hat p =\frac{\hbar}{i}\frac{\partial}{\partial x}p^​=iℏ​∂x∂​. Thus, we get :

⟨p⟩=−iℏ∫−∞∞ψ∗(x,t)∂∂xψ(x,t)dx=−iℏ⟨ψ∣∣∂∂xψ⟩\braket{p} = -i\hbar\int_{-\infty}^\infty \psi^*(x,t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\psi(x,t) dx = -i\hbar \bra{\psi}\ket{\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\psi} ⟨p⟩=−iℏ∫−∞∞​ψ∗(x,t)∂x∂​ψ(x,t)dx=−iℏ⟨ψ∣∣∂x∂​ψ⟩

But remember that ψ(x,t)\psi(x,t)ψ(x,t) can be written in terms of ϕ(k,t)\phi(k,t)ϕ(k,t). This gives :

∂∂xψ=12π∫−∞∞ϕ(k,t)∂∂xeikxdk=i2π∫−∞∞kϕ(k,t)eikxdk=iF−1[kϕ(k,t)]\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \psi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(k,t)\frac{\partial}{\partial x} e^{ikx}dk \\ = \frac{i}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} k \phi(k,t) e^{ikx}dk = i{\cal F}^{-1}[k\phi(k,t)] ∂x∂​ψ=2π​1​∫−∞∞​ϕ(k,t)∂x∂​eikxdk=2π​i​∫−∞∞​kϕ(k,t)eikxdk=iF−1[kϕ(k,t)]

Substituting this back, we get :

⟨p⟩=ℏ⟨ψ∣F−1[kϕ(k,t)]⟩\braket{p} = \hbar \braket{\psi |{\cal F}^{-1} [k \phi(k,t)]} ⟨p⟩=ℏ⟨ψ∣F−1[kϕ(k,t)]⟩

Since the functions we are dealing with are all bounded are analytic, we can switch the order of integration like this :

⟨p⟩=ℏ12π∫−∞∞[∫−∞∞ψ∗(x,t)kϕ(k,t)eikxdx]dk=ℏ∫−∞∞[12π∫−∞∞ψ∗(x,t)eikxdx ]  kϕ(k,t)dk=ℏ∫−∞∞[12π∫−∞∞ψ∗(x,t)eikxdx ]  kϕ(k,t)dk=ℏ∫−∞∞F−1[ψ∗](k,t)  k  ϕ(k,t) dk\braket{p} = \hbar \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^\infty [\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi^*(x,t) k \phi(k,t)e^{ikx}dx]dk \\ = \hbar \int_{-\infty}^\infty [\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi^*(x,t) e^{ikx}dx\,]\; k \phi(k,t) dk \\ = \hbar \int_{-\infty}^\infty [\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\psi^*(x,t) e^{ikx}dx\,]\; k \phi(k,t) dk \\ = \hbar \int_{-\infty}^\infty {\cal F}^{-1}[\psi^*](k,t)\; k\; \phi(k,t) \,dk ⟨p⟩=ℏ2π​1​∫−∞∞​[∫−∞∞​ψ∗(x,t)kϕ(k,t)eikxdx]dk=ℏ∫−∞∞​[2π​1​∫−∞∞​ψ∗(x,t)eikxdx]kϕ(k,t)dk=ℏ∫−∞∞​[2π​1​∫−∞∞​ψ∗(x,t)eikxdx]kϕ(k,t)dk=ℏ∫−∞∞​F−1[ψ∗](k,t)kϕ(k,t)dk

Now, using the conjugation property of fourier transform, i.e. "fourier transform of complex conjugate is complex conjugate of fourier transform", we can write :

⟨p⟩=ℏ∫−∞∞(F−1[ψ])∗kϕ(k,t)dk=ℏ∫−∞∞ϕ∗(k,t)kϕ(k,t)dk  ⟹  ⟨p⟩=ℏ∫−∞∞k∣ϕ(k,t)∣2dk\braket{p} = \hbar \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} ({\cal F}^{-1} [\psi])^* k \phi(k,t) dk \\ = \hbar \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi^*(k,t) k \phi(k,t) dk \implies \\ \braket{p} = \hbar \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} k |\phi(k,t)|^2 dk ⟨p⟩=ℏ∫−∞∞​(F−1[ψ])∗kϕ(k,t)dk=ℏ∫−∞∞​ϕ∗(k,t)kϕ(k,t)dk⟹⟨p⟩=ℏ∫−∞∞​k∣ϕ(k,t)∣2dk

Now, from modern physics, we know that for a particle moving with pomentum ppp, its wavelength is given by λ=h/p\lambda = h/pλ=h/p . This gives the wave number k=2π/λ=2πp/h=p/ℏk = 2\pi/\lambda = 2\pi p/h = p/\hbark=2π/λ=2πp/h=p/ℏ. The solution for V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0V(x,t)=0 is basically a superposition of many plane waves of the form Akei(kx−ωt)A_ke^{i(kx-\omega t)}Ak​ei(kx−ωt) . So of course, we can interpret the ‘‘k"``k"‘‘k" in our equations as the wave-number associated with the De-broglie wavelength.

This leads us to saying that the momentum of each plane wave is given by p=ℏkp = \hbar kp=ℏk. Thus, we should rewrite the equation in a more suggestive form as :

⟨p⟩=∫−∞∞p∣ψ~(p,t)∣2dpwherep=ℏkandψ~(p,t)=1ℏϕ(p/ℏ,t)\braket{p} = \int_{-\infty}^\infty p |\tilde \psi(p,t)|^2 dp \quad \text{where} \quad p = \hbar k \quad \text{and}\quad \tilde \psi(p,t) = \frac{1}{\hbar} \phi(p/\hbar,t) ⟨p⟩=∫−∞∞​p∣ψ~​(p,t)∣2dpwherep=ℏkandψ~​(p,t)=ℏ1​ϕ(p/ℏ,t)

Here, ψ~(p,t)\tilde \psi(p,t)ψ~​(p,t) is what is called the momentum wave function.

Of course, this is more general and not just for a free particle, although the interpretation is most accurate for that case.

Hamiltonian operator

Define the operator

H^=p^22m+V=−ℏ22m∂2∂2x+V\hat H = \frac{\hat p^2}{2m} + V = -\frac{\hbar ^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial ^2 x} + V H^=2mp^​2​+V=−2mℏ2​∂2x∂2​+V

With this, we can write the TDSE as :

H^ψ=iℏ∂∂tψ  ⟺  ∂∂tψ=−iℏH^ψ\hat H \psi = i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi \iff \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi = \frac{-i}{\hbar} \hat H \psi H^ψ=iℏ∂t∂​ψ⟺∂t∂​ψ=ℏ−i​H^ψ

This is similar to the Liouville operator DHD_HDH​ in classical mechanics.

Evolution with time-independent potential

For a lot of systems, V(x,t)=V(x)V(x,t) = V(x)V(x,t)=V(x). Using that, the hamiltonian operator operates entirely in the realm of position. Thus, we can write this :

(∂∂t)(H^)=(H^)(∂∂t)(\frac{\partial}{\partial t})(\hat H) = (\hat H)(\frac{\partial}{\partial t}) (∂t∂​)(H^)=(H^)(∂t∂​)

Thus, we can write:

∂n∂tnH^=H^∂n∂tn  ⟹  ∂n∂tnψ=∂n−1∂tn−1(H^iℏ)ψ=(H^iℏ)∂n−1∂tn−1ψ  ⟹  ∂n∂tnψ=(H^iℏ)nψ\frac{\partial^n}{\partial t^n}\hat H = \hat H \frac{\partial^n}{\partial t^n} \implies \\ \frac{\partial^n}{\partial t^n} \psi = \frac{\partial^{n-1}}{\partial t^{n-1}} (\frac{\hat H}{i\hbar})\psi = (\frac{\hat H}{i\hbar}) \frac{\partial^{n-1}}{\partial t^{n-1}} \psi \implies \frac{\partial^n}{\partial t^n} \psi = (\frac{\hat H}{i\hbar})^n\psi ∂tn∂n​H^=H^∂tn∂n​⟹∂tn∂n​ψ=∂tn−1∂n−1​(iℏH^​)ψ=(iℏH^​)∂tn−1∂n−1​ψ⟹∂tn∂n​ψ=(iℏH^​)nψ

Then, taylor expanding ψ(x,t)\psi(x,t)ψ(x,t) in time, we have :

ψt(x)=ψ(x,t)=10!ψ(x,0)+11!t[∂∂tψ](x,0)+12!t2[∂2∂t2ψ](x,0)+…=[10!ψ](x,0)+[11!(−iℏtH^)ψ](x,0)+[12!(−iℏtH^)2ψ](x,0)+…=[[10!+11!(−iℏtH^)+12!(−iℏtH^)2+… ]ψ](x,0)=[e−itH^/ℏψ](x,0)=e−itH^/ℏψ0\psi_t(x) = \psi(x,t) = \frac{1}{0!}\psi(x,0) + \frac{1}{1!}t[\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\psi](x,0) + \frac{1}{2!}t^2[\frac{\partial^2 }{\partial t^2}\psi](x,0) + \dots \\ = [\frac{1}{0!}\psi](x,0) + [\frac{1}{1!}(\frac{-i}{\hbar}{t\hat H})\psi](x,0) + [\frac{1}{2!}(\frac{-i}{\hbar}{t\hat H})^2\psi](x,0) + \dots \\ = [[\frac{1}{0!} + \frac{1}{1!}(\frac{-i}{\hbar}{t\hat H}) + \frac{1}{2!}(\frac{-i}{\hbar}{t\hat H})^2 + \dots] \psi](x,0) \\ = [e^{-i t\hat H/\hbar}\psi](x,0) = e^{-i t\hat H/\hbar}\psi_0 ψt​(x)=ψ(x,t)=0!1​ψ(x,0)+1!1​t[∂t∂​ψ](x,0)+2!1​t2[∂t2∂2​ψ](x,0)+…=[0!1​ψ](x,0)+[1!1​(ℏ−i​tH^)ψ](x,0)+[2!1​(ℏ−i​tH^)2ψ](x,0)+…=[[0!1​+1!1​(ℏ−i​tH^)+2!1​(ℏ−i​tH^)2+…]ψ](x,0)=[e−itH^/ℏψ](x,0)=e−itH^/ℏψ0​

Thus, we have ψt=e−itH^/ℏψ0\psi_t = e^{-it\hat H/\hbar}\psi_0ψt​=e−itH^/ℏψ0​ . This is again similar to what we got for classical Hamiltonian systems.

Conserved quantities

For any observable with operator O^\hat OO^, it is conserved if it commutes with H^\hat HH^, i.e. H^O^=O^H^\hat H\hat O = \hat O \hat HH^O^=O^H^, so that we may write e−iH^ℏtO^ψ0=O^e−iH^ℏtψ0=O^ψte^{-i\frac{\hat H}{\hbar} t}\hat O \psi_0 = \hat O e^{-i\frac{\hat H}{\hbar} t} \psi_0 = \hat O \psi_te−iℏH^​tO^ψ0​=O^e−iℏH^​tψ0​=O^ψt​ and then ⟨ψ0∣O^∣ψ0⟩=⟨ψt∣O^∣ψt⟩\bra{\psi_0}\hat O\ket{\psi_0} = \bra{\psi_t}\hat O\ket{\psi_t}⟨ψ0​∣O^∣ψ0​⟩=⟨ψt​∣O^∣ψt​⟩ .

Solution of TDSE for time-independent potentials

Now, since we have the case that V(x,t)=V(x)V(x,t) = V(x)V(x,t)=V(x) and thus H^\hat HH^ is an operator in spatial domain, we can use separation of variables to do some nice stuff. First, consider a solution to the TDSE of the form ψ(x,t)=a(x)b(t)\psi(x,t) = a(x)b(t)ψ(x,t)=a(x)b(t) . We can write :

H^ψ=b(t)(H^a)(x)=iℏ∂∂ψ=iℏa(x)b′(t)\hat H \psi = b(t)(\hat H a)(x) = i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial}\psi = i\hbar a(x) b'(t) H^ψ=b(t)(H^a)(x)=iℏ∂∂​ψ=iℏa(x)b′(t)

Then again, when ψ(x,t)≠0\psi(x,t)\ne 0ψ(x,t)=0 we have :

1aH^a=iℏb′/b=E\frac{1}{a}\hat H a =i\hbar b'/b = E a1​H^a=iℏb′/b=E

where EEE is a constant. This gives :

H^a=Eab′=(−iEℏ)b\hat H a = E a \\ b' = (-i\frac{E}{\hbar})b H^a=Eab′=(−iℏE​)b

While the first equation doesn't have a general solution, the solutions of the second one is

b(t)=βe−itEℏb(t) = \beta e^{-it\frac{E}{\hbar}} b(t)=βe−itℏE​

Define ψ(x)=βa(x)\psi(x) = \beta a(x)ψ(x)=βa(x), then we have :

ψ(x,t)=ψ(x)e−itE/ℏH^ψ(x)=Eψ(x)\psi(x,t) = \psi(x) e^{-itE/\hbar} \\ \hat H \psi(x) = E \psi(x) ψ(x,t)=ψ(x)e−itE/ℏH^ψ(x)=Eψ(x)

The second equation is called the time-independent Schrodinger Equation (TISE). Looking closely, the solution ψ(x)\psi(x)ψ(x) for the TISE will be an eigenfunction for the operator H^\hat HH^ with eigenvalue of EEE, which obviously is the Energy of that particular solution. Also notice that for the solution to have the property ⟨ψt∣ψt⟩=1  ∀t\braket{\psi_t|\psi_t} =1 \;\forall t⟨ψt​∣ψt​⟩=1∀t, we need E∈RE \in \mathbb{R}E∈R. A complex value energy also doesn't make any physical sense. Fortunately, this is guaranteed since H^\hat HH^ is a hermitian operator and can only have real valued eigenvalues. Moreover since H^\hat HH^ is a hermitian operator, any two eigenfunctions must either have the same eigenvalue and inner product of 1, or must be orthogonal, i.e. E1≠E2  ⟹  ⟨ψE1∣ψE2⟩=0E_1 \ne E_2 \implies \braket{\psi_{E_1}|\psi_{E_2}}= 0 E1​=E2​⟹⟨ψE1​​∣ψE2​​⟩=0 and E1=E2  ⟹  ⟨ψE1∣ψE2⟩=1E_1=E_2 \implies \braket{\psi_{E_1}|\psi_{E_2}} = 1E1​=E2​⟹⟨ψE1​​∣ψE2​​⟩=1.

Again, this will give us a solution. The good thing is that most of th times, any initial condition, i.e. ψ(x,0)\psi(x,0)ψ(x,0) can be expressed as a linear combination of the (orthonormal) eigenfunctions of H^\hat HH^. Thus, we simply have the general solution given as :

ψ(x,t)=∑−∞∞AEψE(x)e−itE/ℏwhereAE=⟨ψE(x)∣ψ(x,0)⟩\psi(x,t) = \sum_{-\infty}^{\infty} A_E \psi_E(x) e^{-itE/\hbar} \\ \text{where}\quad A_E = \braket{\psi_E(x)|\psi(x,0)} ψ(x,t)=−∞∑∞​AE​ψE​(x)e−itE/ℏwhereAE​=⟨ψE​(x)∣ψ(x,0)⟩

Note that although I denote the basis functions as ψE\psi_EψE​, there can actually be mutiple functions for the same energy level. Using the properties of the eigenbasis, we can choose any function for the inner product in 2nd equation. The only thing compromised will be the uniqueness of the linear combination.

"Split operator" method

Take a look at this equation :

eit2H^/ℏψt=ψt/2=e−it2H^/ℏψ0e^{i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar}\psi_t = \psi_{t/2}= e^{-i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar}\psi_0 ei2t​H^/ℏψt​=ψt/2​=e−i2t​H^/ℏψ0​

We can approximate this for small ttt as :

(1+it2H^/ℏ)ψt≈(1−it2H^/ℏ)ψ0(1+i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar)\psi_t \approx (1 - i\frac{t}{2}\hat H/\hbar)\psi_0 (1+i2t​H^/ℏ)ψt​≈(1−i2t​H^/ℏ)ψ0​

Then, for small xxx, we have :

[∂2∂x2ψ](0,t)≈1x2[ψ(x,t)−2ψ(0,t)+ψ(−x,t)][\frac{\partial ^2}{\partial x^2}\psi](0,t) \approx \frac{1}{x^2}[\psi(x,t) - 2\psi(0,t) + \psi(-x,t)] [∂x2∂2​ψ](0,t)≈x21​[ψ(x,t)−2ψ(0,t)+ψ(−x,t)]

Using this too, we get :

Solving this is going to be a nightmare.

So instead, we approximate even more, giving us what is known as the Alternat Direction Implicit method.

ADI

Here, we split the hamiltonian operator as H^=H^x+H^y\hat H = \hat H_x + \hat H_yH^=H^x​+H^y​ where

H^x=−ℏ2p^x22m+Vx(x,y)H^y=−ℏ2p^y22m+Vy(x,y)\hat H_x = -\frac{\hbar^2 \hat p_x^2}{2m} + V_x(x,y) \\ \hat H_y = -\frac{\hbar^2 \hat p_y^2}{2m} + V_y(x,y) H^x​=−2mℏ2p^​x2​​+Vx​(x,y)H^y​=−2mℏ2p^​y2​​+Vy​(x,y)

It it's possible to separate the potential as V(x,y)=Vx(x)+Vy(y)V(x,y) = V_x(x) + V_y(y)V(x,y)=Vx​(x)+Vy​(y), we can simply split it. Otherwise, we can do Vx=Vy=V/2V_x = V_y = V/2Vx​=Vy​=V/2

Now, for the method, we discretise the wave-function over a grid, giving us the matrix Ψ[y,x]\Psi[y,x]Ψ[y,x]. Just like before, we create the tri-diagonal matrices (using t/2t/2t/2 rather than ttt), but now for each dimension separately. Then we solve :

Ax(y)Ψt/2[y]=Bx(y)Ψ0[y]A_{x}(y)\Psi_{t/2}[y] = B_x(y)\Psi_0[y] Ax​(y)Ψt/2​[y]=Bx​(y)Ψ0​[y]

for all yyy and then

Ay(x)ΨtT[x]=By(x)Ψt/2T[x]A_y(x)\Psi_{t}^T[x] = B_y(x)\Psi_{t/2}^T[x] Ay​(x)ΨtT​[x]=By​(x)Ψt/2T​[x]

for all xxx.

This effectively takes O(MN)O(MN)O(MN) operations each iteration, assuming the grid is M×NM\times NM×N points big.

Atomic Units

For a single electron in first shell of hydrogen atom, we define:

α=14πϵ0qe2ℏc≈1137 andV1=qe24πϵ0a0=ℏ2meV1=4πϵ0ℏ2meqe2=ℏαmec=0.529×10−10 mE0=−V0=V1a0=qe4me(4πϵ0)2ℏ2=α2mec2=27.2eV\alpha = \frac{1}{4\pi \epsilon_0}\frac{q_e^2}{\hbar c} \approx \frac{1}{137}\quad \text{ and} \quad V_1 = \frac{q_e^2}{4\pi \epsilon_0}\\ a_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m_eV_1}= \frac{4\pi \epsilon_0 \hbar^2}{m_e q_e^2} = \frac{\hbar}{\alpha m_e c} = 0.529\times 10^{-10} \text{ m} \\ E_0 = -V_0 = \frac{V_1}{a_0}= \frac{q_e^4 m_e}{(4\pi\epsilon_0)^2 \hbar^2} = \alpha^2m_ec^2 = 27.2 \text{eV} α=4πϵ0​1​ℏcqe2​​≈1371​ andV1​=4πϵ0​qe2​​a0​=me​V1​ℏ2​=me​qe2​4πϵ0​ℏ2​=αme​cℏ​=0.529×10−10 mE0​=−V0​=a0​V1​​=(4πϵ0​)2ℏ2qe4​me​​=α2me​c2=27.2eV

−ℏ22me∂2∂x2ψ+Vψ=iℏ∂∂tV-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \psi + V \psi = i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} V −2me​ℏ2​∂x2∂2​ψ+Vψ=iℏ∂t∂​V

First we substitute x=x~a0x = \tilde x a_0x=x~a0​ and V=V~E0V = \tilde V E_0V=V~E0​, giving :

−ℏ22mea02∂2∂x~2ψ+E0V~ψ=iℏ∂∂tψ-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_ea_0^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \tilde x^2} \psi + E_0\tilde V \psi = i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi −2me​a02​ℏ2​∂x~2∂2​ψ+E0​V~ψ=iℏ∂t∂​ψ

We use the fact that E0a02=a0V1=ℏ2/meE_0a_0^2 = a_0V_1 = \hbar^2/m_eE0​a02​=a0​V1​=ℏ2/me​, giving us :

−12∂2ψ∂x~2+V~ψ=i∂ψ∂t(ℏE0)-\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \tilde x^2} + \tilde V \psi = i \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial t} (\frac{\hbar}{E_0}) −21​∂x~2∂2ψ​+V~ψ=i∂t∂ψ​(E0​ℏ​)

This gives us the A-dimensional Time Dependent Schrodinger Equation (ATDSE) :

−12∂2ψ∂x~2+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂ψ∂t~\boxed{ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial \tilde x^2} + \tilde V \psi = \tilde H \psi = i \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial \tilde t} } −21​∂x~2∂2ψ​+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂t~∂ψ​​

Here H~=1E0H^=−12∂2∂x~2+V~\tilde H = \frac{1}{E_0} \hat H = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \tilde x^2} + \tilde VH~=E0​1​H^=−21​∂x~2∂2​+V~

Once again, assuming V~(x~,t~)=V~(x~)\tilde V(\tilde x,\tilde t) = \tilde V(\tilde x)V~(x~,t~)=V~(x~), we can write :

ψt=eiH^t/ℏψ0=eiH~t~ψ0\psi_t = e^{i\hat H t/\hbar}\psi_0 = e^{i \tilde H \tilde t }\psi_0 ψt​=eiH^t/ℏψ0​=eiH~t~ψ0​

The split operator approximation was:

ψt(x+Δx)+(4mΔx2tℏi−2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)−2)ψt(x)+ψt(x−Δx)≈−ψ0(x+Δx)+(4mΔx2tℏi+2mΔx2ℏ2V(x)+2)ψ0(x)−ψ0(x−Δx)\psi_t(x+\Delta x) + (\frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i - \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) -2)\psi_t(x) + \psi_t(x-\Delta x) \\ \approx \\ - \psi_0(x+\Delta x) + (\frac{4m\Delta x^2}{t\hbar}i + \frac{2m\Delta x^2}{\hbar^2}V(x) + 2)\psi_0(x) - \psi_0(x-\Delta x) ψt​(x+Δx)+(tℏ4mΔx2​i−ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)−2)ψt​(x)+ψt​(x−Δx)≈−ψ0​(x+Δx)+(tℏ4mΔx2​i+ℏ22mΔx2​V(x)+2)ψ0​(x)−ψ0​(x−Δx)

This now becomes:

ψt~(x~+Δx~)+(4Δx~2t~i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2)ψt~(x~)+ψt~(x~−Δx~)≈−ψ0(x~+Δx~)+(4Δx~2t~i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2)ψ0(x~)−ψ0(x~−Δx~)\psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) + (\frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i - 2\Delta \tilde x^2 \tilde V(\tilde x) -2)\psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x) + \psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x) \\ \approx \\ - \psi_0(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) + (\frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i + 2\Delta \tilde x^2 \tilde V(\tilde x) + 2)\psi_0(\tilde x) - \psi_0(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x) ψt~​(x~+Δx~)+(t~4Δx~2​i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2)ψt~​(x~)+ψt~​(x~−Δx~)≈−ψ0​(x~+Δx~)+(t~4Δx~2​i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2)ψ0​(x~)−ψ0​(x~−Δx~)

Similarly for the actual numerical method, now we define

a(x)=4Δx~2t~i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2b(x)=4Δx~2t~i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2a(x) = \frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i - 2\Delta \tilde x^2\tilde V(\tilde x) -2 \\ b(x) = \frac{4\Delta \tilde x^2}{\tilde t}i + 2\Delta \tilde x^2\tilde V(\tilde x) + 2 a(x)=t~4Δx~2​i−2Δx~2V~(x~)−2b(x)=t~4Δx~2​i+2Δx~2V~(x~)+2

Using that, we write :

[1a(x~)1][ψt(x~+Δx~)ψt~(x~)ψt~(x~−Δx~)]=[−1b(x~)−1][ψ0(x~+Δx~)ψ0(x~)ψ0(x~−Δx~)]\begin{bmatrix}1 & a(\tilde x) & 1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\psi_t(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) \\ \psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x) \\ \psi_{\tilde t}(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x)\end{bmatrix} \\ = \\ \begin{bmatrix}-1 & b(\tilde x) & -1\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}\psi_0(\tilde x+\Delta \tilde x) \\ \psi_0(\tilde x) \\ \psi_0(\tilde x-\Delta \tilde x)\end{bmatrix} [1​a(x~)​1​]​ψt​(x~+Δx~)ψt~​(x~)ψt~​(x~−Δx~)​​=[−1​b(x~)​−1​]​ψ0​(x~+Δx~)ψ0​(x~)ψ0​(x~−Δx~)​​

Using this, tri-diagonal matrices A,BA,BA,B will be created, allowing us to do the implicit split-operator step by solving Aψt~=Bψ0A\psi_{\tilde t} = B \psi_0Aψt~​=Bψ0​ in O(N)O(N)O(N) operations using scipy.

For further accuracy, we can even go to a penta-diagonal matrix, using 5-point evaluation of the ∂2∂x2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2}∂x2∂2​ operator.

Leap-Frog like finite difference method

The ATDSE is :

−12∂2∂x~2ψ+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂∂t~ψ- \frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \tilde x^2} \psi + \tilde V \psi= \tilde H \psi = i\frac{\partial }{\partial \tilde t}\psi −21​∂x~2∂2​ψ+V~ψ=H~ψ=i∂t~∂​ψ

Since the H~\tilde HH~ operator can be decomposed lineraly and maps real numbers to real numbers, we can write (after dropping the tilde) :

ψ=R+iI  ⟹  HR+iHI=i∂∂tR−∂∂tI  ⟹  ∂∂tI=HRand∂∂tR=−HI\psi = R + iI \implies \\ H R + i H I= i \frac{\partial }{\partial t} R - \frac{\partial }{\partial t} I \implies \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} I = H R \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial}{\partial t} R = - H I ψ=R+iI⟹HR+iHI=i∂t∂​R−∂t∂​I⟹∂t∂​I=HRand∂t∂​R=−HI

On top of this, we have

∫(I2+R2)dx=1\int (I^2 + R^2) dx = 1 ∫(I2+R2)dx=1

When descritised, this equation becomes

∑x(Ix2+Rx2)=1\sum_x (I_x^2 + R_x^2) = 1 x∑​(Ix2​+Rx2​)=1

Similarly, the evolution equations are discretised in space as :

∂∂tI[x]=V[x]R[x]−121Δx2(R[x+Δx]−2R[x]+R[x−Δx])∂∂tR[x]=−V[x]I[x]+121Δx2(I[x+Δx]−2I[x]+I[x−Δx])\frac{\partial}{\partial t} I[x] = V[x]R[x] - \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\Delta x^2} (R[x+\Delta x]-2R[x]+R[x-\Delta x]) \\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t} R[x] = -V[x]I[x] + \frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{\Delta x^2} (I[x+\Delta x]-2I[x]+I[x-\Delta x]) ∂t∂​I[x]=V[x]R[x]−21​Δx21​(R[x+Δx]−2R[x]+R[x−Δx])∂t∂​R[x]=−V[x]I[x]+21​Δx21​(I[x+Δx]−2I[x]+I[x−Δx])

We can rewrite the first equation as :

∂∂tI[x]=−12Δx2[1−2(1+V[x]Δx2)1][R[x+Δx]R[x]R[x−Δx]]\frac{\partial}{\partial t} I[x] = - \frac{1}{2\Delta x^2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -2(1 + V[x]\Delta x^2) & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} R[x+\Delta x] \\ R[x] \\ R[x-\Delta x] \end{bmatrix} ∂t∂​I[x]=−2Δx21​[1​−2(1+V[x]Δx2)​1​]​R[x+Δx]R[x]R[x−Δx]​​

Define f[x]=−2(1+V[x]Δx2)f[x] = -2(1+V[x]\Delta x^2)f[x]=−2(1+V[x]Δx2) and then the tri-diagonal matrix

F=12Δx2[f[xl]100…001f[xl+Δx]10…0001f[xl+2Δx]1…00⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮0000…1f[xr]]F = \frac{1}{2\Delta x^2}\begin{bmatrix} f[x_l] & 1 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & f[x_l + \Delta x] & 1 & 0 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & f[x_l + 2\Delta x] & 1 & \dots & 0 & 0 \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & 1 & f[x_r] \end{bmatrix} F=2Δx21​​f[xl​]10⋮0​1f[xl​+Δx]1⋮0​01f[xl​+2Δx]⋮0​001⋮0​…………​000⋮1​000⋮f[xr​]​​

Now, vectorising this, with R⃗=[Rx]x\vec R = [R_x]_xR=[Rx​]x​ and I⃗=[Ix]x\vec I = [I_x]_xI=[Ix​]x​, we can write :

∂∂tR⃗=FI⃗∂∂tI⃗=−FR⃗∣∣R⃗∣∣2+∣∣I⃗∣∣2=1\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\vec R = F \vec I\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\vec I = - F \vec R \\ ||\vec R||^2 + ||\vec I||^2 = 1 ∂t∂​R=FI∂t∂​I=−FR∣∣R∣∣2+∣∣I∣∣2=1

This is exactly how the hamiltonian systems we have seen evolve. The third equation is similar to the net energy being constant in a classical mechanics system.

So, just like before, we can use the position verlet LF integrator like so (for small step of size ttt):

R⃗t/2:=R⃗0+t2FI⃗0I⃗t:=I⃗0−tFR⃗t/2R⃗t:=R⃗t/2+t2FR⃗t/2\vec R_{t/2} := \vec R_0 + \frac{t}{2} F \vec I_0 \\ \vec I_{t} := \vec I_0 - t F \vec R_{t/2} \\ \vec R_t := \vec R_{t/2} + \frac{t}{2} F\vec R_{t/2} Rt/2​:=R0​+2t​FI0​It​:=I0​−tFRt/2​Rt​:=Rt/2​+2t​FRt/2​

Effectively what is happening is that

[R⃗t/2I⃗t/2]=[INt2F0NIN][R⃗0I⃗0][R⃗tI⃗t]=[IN0N−t2FIN][R⃗t/2I⃗t/2]\begin{bmatrix} \vec R_{t/2} \\ \vec I_{t/2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{I}_N & \frac{t}{2} \textbf{F}\\ \textbf{0}_N & \textbf{I}_N \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \vec R_{0} \\ \vec I_{0} \end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix} \vec R_{t} \\ \vec I_{t} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{I}_N & \textbf{0}_N \\ - \frac{t}{2} \textbf{F} & \textbf{I}_N \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \vec R_{t/2} \\ \vec I_{t/2} \end{bmatrix} [Rt/2​It/2​​]=[IN​0N​​2t​FIN​​][R0​I0​​][Rt​It​​]=[IN​−2t​F​0N​IN​​][Rt/2​It/2​​]

It's easy to show that both the matrices have a determinant of 1. Thus, the L2 norm is exactly preserved.

But that isn't enough for stability. Instead, for von Neuman or BIBO stability, we require :

t<ΛΔx2t < \Lambda \Delta x^2 t<ΛΔx2

Here, Λ\LambdaΛ is a quantity dependent on V(x)V(x)V(x). For free fall, i.e. V(x)=0V(x)=0V(x)=0, we have Λ=1\Lambda =1Λ=1 . For most other potentials we will encounter, we will have Λ≥1/2\Lambda \ge 1/2Λ≥1/2 .

Thus, as long as t≪12Δx2t \ll \frac{1}{2}\Delta x^2t≪21​Δx2, the simulation will give stable outputs.

Obviously, we won't do the iteration for just the [0,t][0,t][0,t] interval in time, but rather till T=t×NfT = t\times N_fT=t×Nf​ where NfN_fNf​ is number of frames.

The time complexity using either band-matrix multiplication of vector dot products after slicing and padding is O(NNf)O(NN_f)O(NNf​). If Nf≫NN_f \gg NNf​≫N, we can optimise by doing fast matrix exponentiation of the matrix

M:=[IN0N−t2FIN][INt2F0NIN]M := \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{I}_N & \textbf{0}_N \\ - \frac{t}{2} \textbf{F} & \textbf{I}_N \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \textbf{I}_N & \frac{t}{2} \textbf{F}\\ \textbf{0}_N & \textbf{I}_N \end{bmatrix} M:=[IN​−2t​F​0N​IN​​][IN​0N​​2t​FIN​​]

to get MNfM^{N_f}MNf​ in O(N3log⁡Nf)O(N^3 \log N_f)O(N3logNf​) time. For example, if we have (xl,xr)=−10,10(x_l,x_r) = -10,10(xl​,xr​)=−10,10 and Δx=0.1\Delta x = 0.1Δx=0.1, giving us N=201N = 201N=201, but have t=0.001<12Δx2t = 0.001 < \frac{1}{2}\Delta x^2t=0.001<21​Δx2 and we evolve till T1=1T_1=1T1​=1, giving us Nf=1000N_f = 1000Nf​=1000. It may seem that N3≫NNfN^3 \gg N N_fN3≫NNf​ and so this is a waste of time, but pre-computing MNfM^{N_f}MNf​ and repeatedly using it allows us to speed up the simulation by computing effect of NfN_fNf​ iterations via just O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) operations, rather than O(NNf)O(NN_f)O(NNf​). So, if the simulation has to be done for a longer time, say T=1000T=1000T=1000, we can just use the matrix for T=10T=10T=10 and use that to do 100 of 160000-operation matrix-vector multiplications, rather than doing 2×3×2010000002\times 3 \times 2010000002×3×201000000 operations.

This also allows us to make the ttt value really small.

Eventually, there will come a point when

MT/t=(I+tT(M−Int/T))T/t≈exp⁡(Tt(M−In))M^{T/t} = (I+ \frac{t}{T}(\frac{M-\textbf{I}_n}{t/T}))^{T/t} \approx \exp(\frac{T}{t}(M-\textbf{I}_n)) MT/t=(I+Tt​(t/TM−In​​))T/t≈exp(tT​(M−In​))

This quantity can be computed using scipy.linalg.expm in O(N3)O(N^3)O(N3) and is basically the space discretised analogue of the e−iHte^{-iHt}e−iHt operator. Notice I said "space discretised". In the time dimension, it's effectively the solution to the equation

∂∂t[R⃗I⃗]=[0F−F0][R⃗I⃗]\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \begin{bmatrix} \vec R \\ \vec I \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & F \\ -F & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \vec R \\ \vec I \end{bmatrix} ∂t∂​[RI​]=[0−F​F0​][RI​]

i.e.

[R⃗I⃗](T)=exp⁡(TG)([R⃗I⃗](0))whereG=[0F−F0]\begin{bmatrix} \vec R \\ \vec I \end{bmatrix}(T) = \exp(T G) (\begin{bmatrix} \vec R \\ \vec I \end{bmatrix}(0)) \\ \text{where}\quad G = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & F \\ -F & 0 \end{bmatrix} [RI​](T)=exp(TG)([RI​](0))whereG=[0−F​F0​]

It can be shown that as t→0t\to 0t→0, the Tt(M−I)\frac{T}{t}(M-I)tT​(M−I) matrix become GGG. This then raises the obvious question : why bother with leap-frog at all where we can get the time-analytical solution for the space discretised scenario directly ?

Since this has become a very different method from space-discretised leap-frog (SDLP) after all the optimisations and analysis, I will give it a new name: the "Real-Imaginary Split Evolution" (RISE) method.

The algorithm for RISE given Δx,Δt\Delta x, \Delta tΔx,Δt where Δt\Delta tΔt is large, and ψ0,V\psi_0, Vψ0​,V is :

  • Compute f[x]f[x]f[x] from V[x],Δx,ΔtV[x],\Delta x, \Delta tV[x],Δx,Δt
  • Compute FFF and GGG matrices
  • Compute the transition matrix P=exp⁡(GΔt)P = \exp(G\Delta t)P=exp(GΔt)
  • Initialise R=ℜ(ψ0)R = \Re (\psi_0)R=ℜ(ψ0​) and I=ℑ(ψ0)I = \Im(\psi_0)I=ℑ(ψ0​)
  • for each frame:
    • Compute any quantities from ψ=R+iI\psi = R + iIψ=R+iI that are to be tracked (such as ⟨x⟩,⟨p⟩,⟨E⟩,ϕ\braket{x},\braket{p},\braket{E}, \phi⟨x⟩,⟨p⟩,⟨E⟩,ϕ, etc.)
    • Update R,IR,IR,I as [R  I]T:=P[R  I]T[R\;I]^T := P[R\;I]^T[RI]T:=P[RI]T

Although this method gives analytically correct time evolution, the O(N3)O(N^3)O(N3) bottleneck means that the spatial resolution is poor for 2D and 3D cases, and thus the solution will also be in-accurate. Thus, this method isn't used professionally.

But, for the toy examples we have, I can certainly use it to verify correctness.

Shooting method

The TDSE with a time-independent potential can be simplified to the TISE as :

ψE(x,t)=uE(x)e−iEt/ℏ−ℏ22m∂2∂x2uE(x)+V(x)uE(x)=H^uE(x)=EuE(x)whereuE:R→Rand⟨uE∣uE⟩=1\psi_E(x,t) = u_E(x) e^{-iEt/\hbar} \\ -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} u_E(x) + V(x)u_E(x) = \hat H u_E(x) = Eu_E(x) \\ \text{where} \quad u_E : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} \quad \text{and} \quad \braket{u_E | u_E} = 1 ψE​(x,t)=uE​(x)e−iEt/ℏ−2mℏ2​∂x2∂2​uE​(x)+V(x)uE​(x)=H^uE​(x)=EuE​(x)whereuE​:R→Rand⟨uE​∣uE​⟩=1

This means that uE(x)u_E(x)uE​(x) is an eigen-function or eigen-state of H^\hat HH^, with EEE as the eigenvalue, or eigen-energy.

In atomic units, we simply get :

ψE(x~,t~)=uE(x~)e−iE~t~−12∂2∂x~2uE(x~)+V~(x~)uE(x~)=H~uE(x~)=E~u(x~)whereE~=E/E0\psi_E(\tilde x,\tilde t) = u_E(\tilde x)e^{-i\tilde E\tilde t} \\ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \tilde x^2} u_E(\tilde x) + \tilde V(\tilde x) u_E(\tilde x) = \tilde H u_E(\tilde x)= \tilde E u(\tilde x) \\ \text{where} \quad \tilde E = E/E_0 ψE​(x~,t~)=uE​(x~)e−iE~t~−21​∂x~2∂2​uE​(x~)+V~(x~)uE​(x~)=H~uE​(x~)=E~u(x~)whereE~=E/E0​

For the rest of this section, I will be using this adimensional time independent Schrodinger equation (ATISE) without the tilde notation.

Now, consider a potential of the form

V(x)={W(x)ifx∈[xl,xr]0V(x) = \begin{cases} W(x) & \text{if} & x \in [x_l, x_r] \\ 0 \end{cases} V(x)={W(x)0​ifx∈[xl​,xr​]

In this case, for the [xl,xr][x_l, x_r][xl​,xr​] region, we have :

−12d2dx2uE=(E+W(x))uE-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{d x^2} u_E = (E+W(x)) u_E −21​dx2d2​uE​=(E+W(x))uE​

And for the other regions, we have :

−12d2dx2uE=EuE-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{d x^2} u_E = E u_E −21​dx2d2​uE​=EuE​

Now, the solution to −12d2dx2uE=EuE-\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx^2} u_E = E u_E−21​dx2d2​uE​=EuE​ when E<0E < 0E<0, or 2E=−k2, k∈R+2E = -k^2,\, k \in \mathbb{R}^+2E=−k2,k∈R+ is :

uE(x)=Aekx+Be−kxu_E(x) = Ae^{kx} + Be^{-kx} uE​(x)=Aekx+Be−kx

In the region [xr,∞)[x_r, \infty)[xr​,∞), if the AAA coefficient is non-zero, we will have ⟨uE∣uE⟩=∞\braket{u_E|u_E} = \infty⟨uE​∣uE​⟩=∞. This will be non-physical. Similarly, in the (−∞,xl](-\infty, x_l](−∞,xl​] region, if we have B≠0B\ne 0B=0, we face the same issue.

If we instead have E>0E > 0E>0, we will have solutions of the form :

uE(x)=Aeikx+Be−ikxu_E(x) = Ae^{ikx} + Be^{-ikx} uE​(x)=Aeikx+Be−ikx

This immediately has the same problem of ⟨uE∣uE⟩\braket{u_E|u_E}⟨uE​∣uE​⟩ being infinite. Moreover, unlike the E<0E < 0E<0 case, there is no cure to this. Thus, E>0E > 0E>0 is non-physical.

This leaves us with E=0E=0E=0, which gives us uE(x)=Ax+Bu_E(x) = Ax + BuE​(x)=Ax+B. Again, this has the same issue.

Thus, our physical solution for u(x)u(x)u(x) must exponentially decay to 0 as ∣x∣→∞|x| \to \infty∣x∣→∞ for it to be physical.

Although we have figured out these properties only for the particular form of V(x)V(x)V(x) that we used to solve, we can show that the property ∣x∣→∞  ⟹  uE(x)→0|x|\to \infty \implies u_E(x) \to 0∣x∣→∞⟹uE​(x)→0 still holds for any potential that has the proverty ∣x∣→∞  ⟹  V(x)→∞|x|\to \infty \implies V(x) \to \infty∣x∣→∞⟹V(x)→∞. Also, the E<0E<0E<0 property holds too. This is of-course only for a physical solution.

In general, the ATISE has 2 mathematical basis solutions for any E<0E < 0E<0; one physical (like we saw) and other non-physical which grows exponentially on the tails. This is because of the fact that the equation is linear (meaning any solution is a linear combination of a basis of solutions) and 2nd order, meaning that specifying uE(x0)=a,uE′(x0)=bu_E(x_0)=a, u_E'(x_0)=buE​(x0​)=a,uE′​(x0​)=b gives a unique solution. Since, for any (a,b)(a,b)(a,b), we can write it as a linear combination of (uE,physical(x0),uE,physical′(x0))(u_{E,\text{physical}}(x_0), u_{E,\text{physical}}'(x_0))(uE,physical​(x0​),uE,physical′​(x0​)) and (uE,non-physical(x0),uE,non-physical′(x0))(u_{E,\text{non-physical}}(x_0), u_{E,\text{non-physical}}'(x_0))(uE,non-physical​(x0​),uE,non-physical′​(x0​)) for some x0x_0x0​, we can also write any solution as a linear combination of this basis with two elements.

Define xm=12(xr+xl)x_m = \frac{1}{2}(x_r + x_l)xm​=21​(xr​+xl​). Then, one can get a mathematically unique solution for [xm,∞)[x_m, \infty)[xm​,∞) by setting uE(xr)=0u_E(x_r)=0uE​(xr​)=0 and uE′(xr)=vru_E'(x_r)=v_ruE′​(xr​)=vr​. This will be a linear combination of the physical solution that decays to 0 as x→∞x\to \inftyx→∞ and the non-phyiscal solution that explodes ∞\infty∞ instead. Now, by setting vrv_rvr​ as a very small value, the coefficient for the non-physical solution will be small (assuming xrx_rxr​ is large enough) and thus the contribution of the non-physical solution at xmx_mxm​ will be small. This means, that we will effectively recover the value of the physical solution as xmx_mxm​. The same goes for the derivative uE′u_E'uE′​ too (the non-physical solution's contribution to the derivative will be small at xmx_mxm​). Similarly, if we solve for (−∞,xm](-\infty, x_m](−∞,xm​], with uE(xl)=0u_E(x_l)=0uE​(xl​)=0 and uE′(xl)=vlu_E'(x_l)=v_luE′​(xl​)=vl​, the non-physical solution (which explodes to ±∞\pm \infty±∞ as x→∞x\to \inftyx→∞) will have very small contributions at xmx_mxm​ .

Furthermore, the exact values of vlv_lvl​ and vrv_rvr​ only scale the (non-normalised) solutions uE↑,uE↓u_E ^\uparrow, u_E^\downarrowuE↑​,uE↓​ for (−∞,xm](-\infty, x_m](−∞,xm​] and [xm,∞)[x_m, \infty)[xm​,∞) respectively. We know that for the correct values of vrv_rvr​ and vlv_lvl​, the physical solutions for the two halfs will become identical. Again, since this is a 2nd order ODE, this is equivalent to saying

uE↑(xm)=uE↓(xm)uE′↑(xm)=uE′↓(xm)u_E^\uparrow(x_m) = u_E^\downarrow(x_m) \\ u_E'^\uparrow(x_m) = u_E'^\downarrow(x_m) uE↑​(xm​)=uE↓​(xm​)uE′↑​(xm​)=uE′↓​(xm​)

But even without the correct ratio of vr,vlv_r, v_lvr​,vl​, what we do have is :

∃ C∈R   s.t.uE↑(xm)=CuE↓(xm)anduE′↑(xm)=CuE′↓(xm)  ⟹  f(E):=uE↑(xm)uE′↓(xm)−uE↓(xm)uE′↑(xm)=0\exist\, C \in \mathbb{R} \;\text{ s.t.} \quad u_E^\uparrow(x_m) = C u_E^\downarrow(x_m) \quad \text{and} \quad u_E'^\uparrow(x_m) = C u_E'^\downarrow(x_m) \\\implies f(E) := u_E^\uparrow(x_m) u_E'^\downarrow(x_m) - u_E^\downarrow(x_m)u_E'^\uparrow(x_m) = 0 ∃C∈R s.t.uE↑​(xm​)=CuE↓​(xm​)anduE′↑​(xm​)=CuE′↓​(xm​)⟹f(E):=uE↑​(xm​)uE′↓​(xm​)−uE↓​(xm​)uE′↑​(xm​)=0

Of course, for an EEE that is not an eigen-energy, we will have f(E)≠0f(E)\ne 0f(E)=0.

This is the basis for the shooting method. We choose extreme xl,xrx_l, x_rxl​,xr​ values (as per the spatial scale of the problem) and discretise the [xl,xm][x_l, x_m][xl​,xm​] and [xm,xr][x_m, x_r][xm​,xr​] segments. We set the boundary conditions for xl,xrx_l, x_rxl​,xr​ as described, with arbitrary, but small values of vl,vrv_l, v_rvl​,vr​ and solve the 2nd order ODE, for a given energy E<0E<0E<0 for the [xl,xm][x_l, x_m][xl​,xm​] segment and [xm,xr][x_m, x_r][xm​,xr​] segment individually (with the 2nd segment solved backwards from xrx_rxr​ to xmx_mxm​) to get the value of uE↑(xm),uE′↓(xm),uE↓(xm),uE′↑(xm)u_E^\uparrow(x_m),u_E'^\downarrow(x_m),u_E^\downarrow(x_m),u_E'^\uparrow(x_m)uE↑​(xm​),uE′↓​(xm​),uE↓​(xm​),uE′↑​(xm​) and thus f(E)f(E)f(E). Solving the 2nd order ODE can be done using any method, say RK2. The goal is to verify whether EEE is an eigen-energy by checking whether f(E)≈0f(E)\approx 0f(E)≈0.

Although, we can zero-in on a particular eigen-energy using bisection methods in log⁡2(NE)\log_2(N_E)log2​(NE​) time were NEN_ENE​ is the number of values of EEE (regularly spaced) that we will test. I instead want to create plots for f(E)f(E)f(E) itself. To do this, I will define:

u⃗(x)=[uEk(x)]kv⃗(x)=[uEk′(x)]kE⃗=[Ek]k\vec u(x) = [u_{E_k}(x)]_k \\ \vec v(x) = [u'_{E_k}(x)]_k \\ \vec E = [E_k]_k u(x)=[uEk​​(x)]k​v(x)=[uEk​′​(x)]k​E=[Ek​]k​

and re-write the ATISE as :

ddxv⃗(x)=2(V(x)−E⃗)∗u⃗(x)=K(x)⃗∗u⃗(x)=a⃗(x)ddxu⃗(x)=v(x)\frac{d}{dx} \vec v(x) = 2(V(x)-\vec E)* \vec u(x) = \vec{K(x)}*\vec u(x) = \vec a(x)\\ \frac{d}{dx} \vec u(x) = v(x) dxd​v(x)=2(V(x)−E)∗u(x)=K(x)​∗u(x)=a(x)dxd​u(x)=v(x)

Here, the "∗*∗" symbol represents point-wise multiplication.

To make the method memory efficient, we will simply update the vectors via the RK2 step as well as the xxx value (by chosen Δx\Delta xΔx) till xmx_mxm​ is reached. We will do this for both the halfs of the [xl,xr][x_l, x_r][xl​,xr​] segment individually and then compute the vector f⃗=[f(Ek)]k\vec f = [f(E_k)]_kf​=[f(Ek​)]k​ from the resulting vectors at xmx_mxm​.

We will also implement a separate function that will run RK2 for a given (scalar) xl,xr,Δx,a(x),vl,ulx_l, x_r, \Delta x, a(x), v_l, u_lxl​,xr​,Δx,a(x),vl​,ul​ and will go all the way from xlx_lxl​ to xrx_rxr​ with no split like we did for the shooting method. It will fill an array for uuu in the process (initially set to all 0) and return this array as the result. This function will be used to visualise the eigenstates by passing in the corresponding a(x)a(x)a(x).

Central attractive potentials in 3D

Consider the 3D ATDSE with a central attractive potential V(r)V(r)V(r) where r=∣r∣r = |r|r=∣r∣:

−12∇2ψ(r⃗,t)+V(r)ψ(r⃗,t)=i∂∂tψ(r⃗,t)-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2\psi(\vec r, t) + V(r)\psi(\vec r,t) = i\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\psi(\vec r, t) −21​∇2ψ(r,t)+V(r)ψ(r,t)=i∂t∂​ψ(r,t)

We can, as always, convert this to a time-independent equation as :

−12∇2ψ(r⃗)+V(r)ψ(r⃗)=Eψ(r⃗)-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2\psi(\vec r) + V(r)\psi(\vec r) = E\psi(\vec r) −21​∇2ψ(r)+V(r)ψ(r)=Eψ(r)

Now, futher doing a separation of variables as ψ(r⃗)=R(r)Y(α,β)\psi(\vec r) = R(r)Y(\alpha, \beta)ψ(r)=R(r)Y(α,β) (where α\alphaα is the angle from the z axes and β\betaβ is the polar angle in the x-y plane) and using the spherical coordinate version of the laplacian, i.e.

∇2=1r2∂∂rr2∂∂r+1r21sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂α+1r21sin⁡2α∂2∂β2\nabla^2 = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r} r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} + \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{1}{\sin^2 \alpha}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2} ∇2=r21​∂r∂​r2∂r∂​+r21​sinα1​∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​+r21​sin2α1​∂β2∂2​

we can write :

∇2ψ(r⃗)=[1r2∂∂rr2∂∂rR]Y+[1r2R][1sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αY+1sin⁡2α∂2∂β2Y]=2(V(r)−E)RY\nabla^2 \psi(\vec r) = [\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial }{\partial r} r^2 \frac{\partial}{\partial r} R]Y + [\frac{1}{r^2}R][\frac{1}{\sin \alpha}\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin \alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} Y + \frac{1}{\sin^2 \alpha}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2} Y] = 2(V(r)-E)RY ∇2ψ(r)=[r21​∂r∂​r2∂r∂​R]Y+[r21​R][sinα1​∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​Y+sin2α1​∂β2∂2​Y]=2(V(r)−E)RY

For the cases where ψ≠0,r≠0\psi \ne 0, r \ne 0ψ=0,r=0, we can write :

Clearly, since LHS and RHS are functions of different coordinates, they must both be a constant, say some LLL. This gives :

LR=2r2R(V−E)−ddrr2ddrRLYsin⁡2α=sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αY+∂2∂β2YLR = 2r^2R(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr}r^2 \frac{d}{dr}R \\ LY\sin^2\alpha = \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} Y + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2}Y LR=2r2R(V−E)−drd​r2drd​RLYsin2α=sinα∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​Y+∂β2∂2​Y

Now, as we have arbitrary scaling for each part, we can WLOG assume that the angular part is normalised. Essentially, we require :

∫r=−∞∞∫α∫βR(r)2Y2(α,β)r2sin⁡αdrdαdβ=1  ⟹  [∫−∞∞R2(r)r2dr][∫α∫βY2(α,β)sin⁡αdαdβ]=1\int_{r=-\infty}^\infty\int_\alpha\int_\beta R(r)^2Y^2(\alpha,\beta) r^2\sin\alpha dr d\alpha d\beta = 1 \\\implies [\int_{-\infty}^\infty R^2(r)r^2 dr][\int_{\alpha}\int_\beta Y^2(\alpha,\beta) \sin\alpha d\alpha d\beta] =1 ∫r=−∞∞​∫α​∫β​R(r)2Y2(α,β)r2sinαdrdαdβ=1⟹[∫−∞∞​R2(r)r2dr][∫α​∫β​Y2(α,β)sinαdαdβ]=1

we can then have the normalisation

Then, for the expected value of any function g(r)g(r)g(r), we can do

⟨g⟩=∫r=−∞∞∫α∫βg(r)R2(r)Y2(α,β)r2sin⁡αdrdαdβ=∫−∞∞g(r)R2(r)r2dr\braket{g} = \int_{r=-\infty}^\infty\int_\alpha\int_\beta g(r)R^2(r)Y^2(\alpha,\beta) r^2\sin\alpha dr d\alpha d\beta \\= \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(r)R^2(r)r^2 dr ⟨g⟩=∫r=−∞∞​∫α​∫β​g(r)R2(r)Y2(α,β)r2sinαdrdαdβ=∫−∞∞​g(r)R2(r)r2dr

Now, once again, we can split Y=P(α)Q(β)Y=P(\alpha)Q(\beta)Y=P(α)Q(β), allowing us to rewite the 2nd equation as ;

L[Psin⁡2α]Q=[sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αP]Q+P[∂2∂β2Q]L[P\sin^2\alpha]Q = [\sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha}\sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} P]Q + P[\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta^2}Q] L[Psin2α]Q=[sinα∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​P]Q+P[∂β2∂2​Q]

Then, once again, by the same logic, we can write :

LPsin⁡2α−sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αP=PM∂2∂2β2Q=QMLP\sin^2\alpha - \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} P = PM \\ \frac{\partial^2}{\partial^2\beta^2}Q = QM LPsin2α−sinα∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​P=PM∂2β2∂2​Q=QM

where MMM is some constant.

In summary, we have this eigenstate :

ψE,L,M(r⃗)=R(r)P(α)Q(β)LR=2r2R(V−E)−ddrr2ddrRLPsin⁡2α−sin⁡α∂∂αsin⁡α∂∂αP=PM∂2∂2β2Q=QM\boxed{\psi_{E,L,M}(\vec r) = R(r)P(\alpha)Q(\beta)}\\ \boxed{LR = 2r^2R(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr}r^2 \frac{d}{dr}R} \\ \boxed{LP\sin^2\alpha - \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} \sin\alpha \frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha} P = PM} \\ \boxed{\frac{\partial^2}{\partial^2\beta^2}Q = QM} ψE,L,M​(r)=R(r)P(α)Q(β)​LR=2r2R(V−E)−drd​r2drd​R​LPsin2α−sinα∂α∂​sinα∂α∂​P=PM​∂2β2∂2​Q=QM​

For the last equation, since β∈[0,2π]\beta \in [0,2\pi]β∈[0,2π], and the solution must be periodic for it to be physical, we require M=−m2M=-m^2M=−m2 where mmm is an integer, giving us e±imβe^{\pm i m\beta}e±imβ as the basis. This ‘‘m"``m"‘‘m" is called the Azimuthal Quantum Number. Similarly for the equation involving P(α)P(\alpha)P(α), it turns out that we require L=−l(l+1)L = -l(l+1)L=−l(l+1) where lll is an integer. This ‘‘l"``l"‘‘l" is the Orbital Angular Momentum Quantum Number .

The lll quantum number gives us the shape of the "orbit" and the mmm quantum number gives us the orientation.

For example, if m=0m=0m=0, we get rotational symmetry about z axis, like in the case of the pzp_zpz​ orbital . If it is non-zero, we get a sinusoidal basis, i.e. sin⁡(mβ)\sin(m\beta)sin(mβ) and cos⁡(mβ)\cos(m\beta)cos(mβ) . For example, with m2=1m^2=1m2=1, we have sin⁡(β),cos⁡(β)\sin(\beta),\cos(\beta)sin(β),cos(β). These basis functions are what chemists (not physicists) denote as the m=1m=1m=1 and m=−1m=-1m=−1 states. That is ofc, utter garbarge notation. But that's just what is used.

Now, substituting L=−l(l+1)L = -l(l+1)L=−l(l+1) back into the equation for RRR, we get :

−l(l+1)R=2r2R(V−E)−ddrr2ddrR-l(l+1)R = 2r^2R(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr}r^2 \frac{d}{dr}R −l(l+1)R=2r2R(V−E)−drd​r2drd​R

Define u(r)=rR(r)  ⟹  R=u/ru(r)=rR(r) \implies R = u/ru(r)=rR(r)⟹R=u/r, giving us :

−l(l+1)ur=2ru(V−E)−ddr(ru′−u)  ⟹  −l(l+1)u=2r2u(V−E)−r(ru′′+u′−u′)  ⟹  u′′(r)=(2(V(r)−E)+l(l+1)r2) u(r)-l(l+1)\frac{u}{r} = 2ru(V-E) - \frac{d}{dr} (ru' -u) \\\implies -l(l+1)u = 2r^2u(V-E) - r (ru'' + u' - u') \\\implies \boxed{u''(r) = (2(V(r)-E) +\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}) \,u(r)} −l(l+1)ru​=2ru(V−E)−drd​(ru′−u)⟹−l(l+1)u=2r2u(V−E)−r(ru′′+u′−u′)⟹u′′(r)=(2(V(r)−E)+r2l(l+1)​)u(r)​

This is accompanied by the normalisation condition

∫−∞∞u2(r)dr=1\int_{-\infty}^\infty u^2(r)dr = 1 ∫−∞∞​u2(r)dr=1

and the expectation equation (assuming normalisation is done) :

⟨g(r)⟩=∫−∞∞g(r)u2(r)dr\braket{g(r)} = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g(r)u^2(r)dr ⟨g(r)⟩=∫−∞∞​g(r)u2(r)dr

Now, consider the a-dimensionalised electrostratic potential for an electron in some shell of a hydrogen atom, i.e. V(r)=−1/rV(r) = -1/rV(r)=−1/r. Plugging that in, we get :

u′′(r)=(−2E−2r+l(l+1)r2)u(r)  ⟺  −12d2dr2u(r)+[l(l+1)2r2−1r]u(r)=Eu(r)u''(r) = (-2E - \frac{2}{r} + \frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}) u(r) \iff\\ \boxed{-\frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2}{dr^2} u(r) + [\frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} - \frac{1}{r}]u(r) = Eu(r)} u′′(r)=(−2E−r2​+r2l(l+1)​)u(r)⟺−21​dr2d2​u(r)+[2r2l(l+1)​−r1​]u(r)=Eu(r)​

The boxed equation is what the assignment refers to as the "radial equation" (though it's using u=rRu = rRu=rR and not RRR).

Define

Veff(r)=V(r)+l(l+1)2r2V_\text{eff}(r) = V(r) + \frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} Veff​(r)=V(r)+2r2l(l+1)​

This in our case is:

Veff(r)=−1r+l(l+1)2r2V_\text{eff}(r) = -\frac{1}{r} + \frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} Veff​(r)=−r1​+2r2l(l+1)​

Using this, we can rewrite the equation as :

u′′(r)=2(V(r)−E)u(r)  ⟺  −12d2dr2u(r)+Veffu(r)=Eu(r)u''(r) = 2(V(r)-E) u(r) \iff \\ -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dr^2} u(r) + V_\text{eff} u(r) = E u(r) u′′(r)=2(V(r)−E)u(r)⟺−21​dr2d2​u(r)+Veff​u(r)=Eu(r)

This is similar to the usual TISE formulation, although u(r)u(r)u(r) is not really the wave function we want to finally be solving for.

Since the assignment asks to modify the potential in one of the parts, let us consider a more general potential of

V(r)=−Ze−μrr+λr2  ⟹  Veff(r)=−Ze−μrr+λr2+l(l+1)2r2V(r) = -\frac{Ze^{-\mu r}}{r} + \lambda r^2 \\\implies V_\text{eff}(r) = -\frac{Ze^{-\mu r}}{r} + \lambda r^2 + \frac{l(l+1)}{2r^2} V(r)=−rZe−μr​+λr2⟹Veff​(r)=−rZe−μr​+λr2+2r2l(l+1)​

This is what we will use for the implementation. Namely, we will have the function:

def electrostatic_potential_eff(r:(np.ndarray|float), l=0, mu=0, lamb=0, Z=1):
    return (lamb*r*r) + (l*(l+1)/((2*r*r) + 1e-30)) - (Z*np.exp(-mu*r)/(r+1e-30))

Shooting method for cental potentials

The function that will be written for the shooting method will accept any potential V:R→RV:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}V:R→R as an input. We will simply pass in electrostatic_potential_eff as an input to simulate an atom with atomic number ZZZ and a single electron.

Now, it's worth noting that since we cannot integrate over r=0r=0r=0, our interval [rl,rr][r_l, r_r][rl​,rr​] must lie in the r>0r>0r>0 region entirely. This is different from the assumptions we made while developing the Shooting method. In particular, we assumed that xl,xrx_l, x_rxl​,xr​ are extreme values, for which the physical solution will have small value and derivative, while the non-physical solution will have values with large magnitudes. Here, though rlr_lrl​ is not an extreme, it still has the property we need, namely that the physical solution for u(r)=rR(r)u(r)=rR(r)u(r)=rR(r) will have a small value (though R(r)R(r)R(r) may not have small values) and the non-physical solution, which has the asymptotics of r−lr^{-l}r−l will have a large values.

Even then, there's another issue. When we integrate numerically, every step, there is some numerical error ϵ\epsilonϵ that gets added to the solution. This noise is auto-regressive, since the noise added prior to a particular step will be amplified by the numbers that u(r),v(r)u(r),v(r)u(r),v(r) are multiplied with. If not careful, this can cause the noise to overtake the actual solution and explode. To prevent this, a smaller Δx\Delta xΔx is usually used, at the expense of computational cost. In our case, since there is a singularity at r=0r=0r=0, even if the actual solution doesn't explode to infinity, if we start integrating close to the singularity with a Δx\Delta xΔx that is not adequately small, the numerical solution will explode. This effect is particularly promininent near the "classical turning point" rcr_crc​ where Veff(rc)−E=0V_\text{eff}(r_c)-E = 0Veff​(rc​)−E=0, i.e. the inflection point for uuu. So, to prevent the noise from over-whelming the numerical solution, we must integrate in the regions [rl,rc][r_l, r_c][rl​,rc​] and [rc,rr][r_c, r_r][rc​,rr​] and must have as high accuracy for the step-size as possible.

Now, with the O(Δx4)O(\Delta x^4)O(Δx4) accuracy of the Numerov method, we can still use the midpoint rm=(rl+rr)/2r_m = (r_l+r_r)/2rm​=(rl​+rr​)/2 as the matching point, rather than rcr_crc​.

In fact, mathematically (assuming perfect integrator), it doesn't matter what we choose as the matching point; the f(E)f(E)f(E) value will remain the same since the two solutions (uniquely determined by initial conditions) remain the same, and the matching loss function is actually a special quantity called the Wronskian. In particular,

f(E)=WE(xm)=∣uE↑(xm)uE↓(xm)vE↑(xm)vE↓(xm)∣f(E) = W_E(x_m)= \begin{vmatrix} u_E^{\uparrow}(x_m) & u_E^{\downarrow}(x_m) \\ v_E^{\uparrow}(x_m) & v_E^{\downarrow}(x_m) \end{vmatrix} f(E)=WE​(xm​)=​uE↑​(xm​)vE↑​(xm​)​uE↓​(xm​)vE↓​(xm​)​​

This can be shown to be invariant w.r.t xmx_mxm​.

Moreover this quantity is 0 only when the two solutions are linearly dependent, i.e. they are multiples of each other. This is effectively saying that (after normalisation), they are the same solutions (save for a sign flip).
